item.title: Geometry-controlled active transport in smectic textures
item.description: arXiv:2610.37812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-propelled particles moving through structured anisotropic media such as smectic liquid crystals exhibit transport properties that differ qualitatively from those in isotropic environments. Here we introduce a minimal model of an active Brownian particle whose propulsion axis is coupled to the layer-normal field of a smectic liquid crystal. Using numerical simulations complemented by approximate analytical calculations, we investigate the dynamics of an active particle in three representative two-dimensional smectic microstructures: a uniform planar texture, an isolated toroidal focal conic domain, and a periodic array of toroidal focal conic domains. For the planar and isolated focal-conic geometries, we characterize the crossover from short-time superdiffusion to long-time normal diffusion. In periodic focal-conic arrays, however, transport is controlled by two distinct persistence mechanisms whose relative importance depends on the P\'eclet number ($\mathrm{Pe}$) and the coupling strength $\varepsilon$ between the particle orientation and the smectic layer-normal field. At small $\varepsilon$, long-time diffusion is governed by the intrinsic persistence time of the active Brownian dynamics. At large $\varepsilon$, repeated scattering by smectic defects generates an emergent persistence time that dominates the transport. These results demonstrate that the competition between the intrinsic persistence of active motion and the mean free time between encounters with smectic defects provides a simple physical mechanism for the emergence of nontrivial diffusive behavior in structured anisotropic media.
item.dc:creator: Yhony M. Arce, William G. C. Oropesa, Alef R. Siqueira, Hartmut L\"owen, Andr\'e P. Vieira, Danilo B. Liarte

item.title: Structural Determination vs Stochastic Events: Relaxation Dynamics in a Supercooled Liquid
item.description: arXiv:2610.38375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural relaxation in supercooled liquids is influenced by the initial configuration, yet its microscopic evolution exhibits substantial variability. Here, we investigate the interplay between structural constraints and dynamical stochasticity by examining fluctuations of relaxation dynamics across and within isoconfigurational ensembles. We show that fluctuations among trajectories originating from the same configuration constitute a substantial fraction of the total dynamical fluctuations over a broad range of temperatures. At the collective level, the distribution of relaxation times is well described by a stochastic model involving a sequence of effective relaxation events, whose number decreases upon cooling. At the microscopic level, dynamical fluctuations exhibit spatial correlations that grow upon cooling, revealing a spatial organization of relaxation even when the initial configuration is fixed. Remarkably, the characteristic length associated with these fluctuations closely follows the length scale inferred from the stochastic first-passage model, establishing a connection between the spatial organization of dynamical fluctuations and the temporal statistics of collective relaxation. Together, these results suggest that structural relaxation is governed by an interplay between configuration-dependent constraints and stochastic dynamical events: the initial structure influences when and where relaxation occurs, without uniquely determining its microscopic realization.
item.dc:creator: Shivam Mahajan, Peter Harrowell, Massimo Pica Ciamarra

item.title: Extraordinary stiffening and reciprocal control in a DNA condensate/actin composite
item.description: arXiv:2610.38504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft composites, materials consisting of inclusions within a polymeric matrix, offer a broad design space with diverse mechanical properties. Composite stiffness is normally set by the volume fraction of filler, and classical theory predicts at most ~25% stiffening when inclusions occupy 10% of the volume. Here we introduce a composite of phase-separated DNA droplets that occupy <10% of an entangled actin network, yet stiffen it 25-fold, reversibly. Microscopy reveals that actin penetrates the DNA droplets, leading network elasticity to determine their size; thus the system exhibits reciprocal control between matrix and droplet properties. We attribute the extraordinary stiffening to entrainment of actin by the droplets, which enlarges the effective inclusions until their contact network dominates the mechanics. This shows that liquid-liquid phase separation can control not only local compositions, but also mechanics, achieving exceptional stiffening at modest filler fractions through local geometries that constrain the matrix beyond the inclusions themselves.
item.dc:creator: Sam Wilken, Austin Hopkins, Kyu Hwan Choi, John Berezney, Matthew E. Helgeson, M. Cristina Marchetti, Sho Takatori, Zvonimir Dogic, Omar A. Saleh

item.title: The effects of hydrodynamic interactions on the swimming velocity and stability of a swarm of microswimmers
item.description: arXiv:2610.38689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dynamics and stability of a swarm of microswimmers is examined here using a thermodynamically compliant microswimmer model. The theory presented here is a mean-field model in which the swarm is considered to be a uniform solution of swimmers that are moving, on average, in the same direction. The hydrodynamic interaction between swimmers is modeled accurately assuming a crystalline arrangement to the swarm. A swimmer in the swarm can swim up to twelve times faster than when alone in an infinite sea, when the volume fraction of swimmers in the swarm is about 0.14. Moreover we have also studied the stability of the swarm around a uniform crystalline arrangement by calculating the hydrodynamic torques generated by the swarm as a function of the volume fraction of swimmers. The predictions presented here agree with recent multiparticle simulations that have shown that hydrodynamic torques have a stabilizing effect in swarms of pullers while swarms of pushers are generally destabilized by hydrodynamic interactions. The thermodynamically admissible coupling between the swimmer's motion and fuel consumption allows us to study the full dynamics instead of artificially constrained steady-states only. By accounting for fuel consumption and high order hydrodynamic interactions we are able to examine the swarm's stability as function of fuel concentration and the volume fraction of swimmers. We find that at high concentrations of fuel, swarms of pullers are stabilized by hydrodynamic torques for volume fractions of swimmers as low as 0.02 but at lower volume fractions Brownian forces make the swarm unstable.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'{e}s C\'{o}rdoba, Jay D. Schieber

item.title: Nonreciprocity Propels Nematic Defects
item.description: arXiv:2610.39037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonreciprocal interactions are a generic source of nonequilibrium dynamics, yet their consequences for nematic topological defects remain unexplored. We introduce a nonreciprocal nematic model on a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice and formulate a continuum theory containing a nematic nonreciprocal torque. In the deterministic limit, simulations and symmetry analysis show that this torque drives +1/2 defects to self-propel along their polar axes. Nonreciprocity modifies the splitting pathway of integer +1 defects. These results identify a symmetry-resolved route from nonreciprocity to nematic defect transport and topological reorganization, distinct from active-stress-driven motion.
item.dc:creator: Yunpeng Cao, Yu Du, Yao Li

item.title: Response of Hydrogels and Microgels to Nanoparticle Crowding
item.description: arXiv:2610.39039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internal degrees of freedom of cross-linked polymer networks enable compressible hydrogels and microgels to swell or deswell by absorbing or expelling solvent in response to environmental changes. Macromolecules in solution can influence the swelling response by acting as crowding agents, with practical relevance for drug delivery and biosensing. We extend the Flory-Rehner theory of polymer network swelling to incorporate nanoparticle crowders as another implicit species that can perturb a gel through volume exclusion, including the entropic cost of crowder penetration from polymer field theory. Within the free energy landscape of asymmetric ternary mixtures, we numerically solve equilibrium relations equating solvent and crowder chemical potentials inside and outside the gel. Independently, we perform Monte Carlo simulations, including trial moves that allow gels to swell and take up crowders. We investigate how crowder size, solution concentration, cross-link density, and solvent quality influence swelling of polymeric gels, partitioning of crowders between inside and outside, and structural properties of microgel suspensions governed by Hertzian elastic pair interactions. Our results show that nanoparticle crowding promotes deswelling, thereby weakening interparticle correlations, and that, with increasing the concentration of crowders, polymeric gels reach a maximum loading capacity, dependent on crowder size and polymer cross-link density.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Mahesh Aryal and Alan R. Denton, J. Chem. Phys. 164, 064904 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Mahesh Aryal, Alan R. Denton

item.title: The End of Chaos at the Ideal Glass Transition
item.description: arXiv:2610.39098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ideal glass transition has often been associated with the extrapolated vanishing of configurational entropy $S_c$, yet how this thermodynamic criterion is reflected in microscopic dynamics remains unclear. Here, we show that the vanishing of deterministic chaos quantified by the maximum Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}$ provides such a dynamical signature. Using molecular dynamics simulations across diverse model glass-forming liquids in two and three dimensions, we show that $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}$ follows an approximate scaling $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}} \propto (T-T_{\lambda})^{1/2}$ and extrapolates to zero at a temperature $T_{\lambda}$ consistent with the Kauzmann temperature $T_{\mathrm{K}}$. Furthermore, we establish the quantitative relation $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}^2 \propto T S_c$, directly linking chaotic dynamics to configurational entropy. By demonstrating that $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}^2 \propto \sigma_K^2$, where $\sigma_K^2$ is the variance of local potential energy landscape curvature fluctuations, we connect the suppression of chaos directly to landscape geometry. These results provide a unified thermodynamic, dynamical, and geometric framework for glass formation, identifying the ideal glass transition as the endpoint of chaotic exploration of the energy landscape.
item.dc:creator: Zi-Long Wang, Jack F. Douglas, Matteo Baggioli, Zhao-Yan Sun, Wen-Sheng Xu

item.title: Aging and protocol dependence of thermal activation events in structural glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.39405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, we investigate the waiting time dependence and the protocol dependence of thermally activated events in structural glasses using molecular simulations and potential energy landscape analysis. We find a qualitative crossover in the nature of activation events; from avalanche-like events to local events. We also use the isoconfigurational ensemble analysis and reveal that the events become less diverse and more reversible. We discuss these crossovers from the perspective of the stability and the potential energy landscape of glasses. To investigate the protocol dependence, we compare the two types of glasses whose stability is controlled by waiting time and parent temperature, respectively. Surprisingly, at the same inherent structure energy level, the parent-temperature-controlled glasses are more unstable and maintain their avalanche-like nature. These results demonstrate that the activation properties of structural glasses are not determined solely by their energy levels, highlighting the essential role of state connectivity and the dynamical sampling in the complex energy landscape.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Takaha, Atsushi Ikeda

item.title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.39465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clay films that dry on a rigid substrate crack, peel or stay intact, and which of these happens matters for coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing. Composites of clay with polymers have been studied widely. Clay composites, whose components differ in size and charge, are much less explored. We show that mixing the nano scale clay Laponite with the micron scale clay Bentonite reduces desiccation damage on both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic substrate, Laponite films stay essentially intact, Bentonite films fracture extensively, and on glass most intermediate compositions are less damaged than a simple average of the two would suggest. Rheology of the gelled suspensions reveals a two step yielding in every composition, and the cohesive energy derived from it depends by orders of magnitude on which step is used, a point that any rheology cracking correlation must specify. A dimensionless cohesion adhesion index, whose sign we derive from an energy balance, is consistent with compositions that peel on polypropylene and crack on glass. Replicate experiments were performed for robustness of results. The results identify composition as a simple handle on the crack resistance of clay films and open the search for the critical crack-free thickness as a function of clay composition.
item.dc:creator: Tapati Dutta, Agnishikha Chakrabarti, Soham Mitra, Deepshikha Das, Indranil Chakraborty

item.title: Hidden Phase Transition in Single-Polymer Stretching under Elongational Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.39575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model reproduces both transitions and shows that they are phase transitions in the long-chain limit. Single-molecule DNA experiments provide qualitative support for the dynamical transition through the predicted reversal of the folding response.
item.dc:creator: Aiqing Zhu, Fushuai Wang, Eleonore Vissol-Gaudin, Qianxiao Li, Beatrice W. Soh

item.title: Temporal Correlations and Optimal Feedback Control of an Active Information Engine
item.description: arXiv:2610.39632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much does a feedback controller need to know about the fluctuations it exploits? We address this question using a macroscopic information engine driven by self-propelled bristle-robots. Experimentally measured occupancy time series show that temporal correlations strongly affect vacancy detection. At short measurement intervals, mean first-passage times exceed independent-measurement predictions by more than an order of magnitude. A first-order Markov approximation captures much of this effect. It does not reproduce the full first-passage distribution, revealing higher-order temporal memory. Nevertheless, Markov-selected protocols come within 0.15\% of the maximum experimental power. Neglecting correlations causes power losses of several percent and favors larger compression distances. Introducing a sensing cost shifts the optimal strategy toward sparse sensing. The independent model cannot predict this shift, whereas the Markov model captures it. Cross-validation on separate time segments confirms the near-optimal performance of Markov-selected protocols. These findings demonstrate that near-optimal feedback control in correlated nonequilibrium systems can require a simpler statistical description than predicting their full temporal dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Laura Hoek, Yael Roichman

item.title: Influence of hydrophobic polyelectrolyte composition on pH-dependent solubilization of lipid bilayer membranes
item.description: arXiv:2610.39736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lipid bilayer membranes can be solubilized in the form of disks of approximately 10 nm in diameter by several types of hydrophobic polyelectrolytes (HPE). The disks are stabilized by wrapped HPE along the rims of the disks. We compare the solubilization behavior of anionic HPE with chain lengths in between 20 - 100 monomers, and with varying molecular composition. We find that (1) HPE as short as 20 monomers can readily solubilize lipid bilayer membranes; (2) spatial intermolecular arrangement of ionic and hydrophobic groups in HPE determine if solubilization occurs; (3) anionic HPEs may exhibit two distinct pH-dependent solubilization transitions: the first is encountered in the lower-pH regime upon increasing the pH, whereas the second emerges at higher pH when the pH is decreased; (4) a binomial composition distribution of hydrophobic and ionizable groups over the chains, compared to a fixed composition, does not lead to a measurably wider pH range where solubilization occurs for the transition at low pH. We link the solubilization behavior of one of the HPE's to pH-dependent partitioning between macroscopic oil and water phases. Finally, (5) we find that linear composition superposition of the hydrophobic groups in HPE quantitatively accounts for the composition dependence of the pH's where solubilization occurs. This result holds within a range of compositions and breaks down below a critical fraction of hydrophobic residues in a HPE chain. Throughout, we compare the observations to a recently developed model for ligand-mediated cooperative transitions. Our findings have potential impact on anti-cancer medicine and drug delivery applications.
item.dc:creator: Martijn Koorengevel, Michelle N. M. de Dood, Wouter T. E. Bosker, James L. Martin Robinson, Cornelis A. van Walree, Bas G. P. van Ravensteijn, Willem K. Kegel

item.title: High-throughput quantification of interfacial protein load in monodisperse oil-in-water emulsions
item.description: arXiv:2610.40506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Food proteins play a critical role as emulsifiers, where adsorption at the oil and water interface governs emulsion formation and stability. However, quantitative characterization of interfacial protein load remains challenging due to polydispersity in conventional emulsification methods. We combine microfluidic generation of monodisperse emulsions with colorimetric protein quantification to measure the post-collection initial interfacial load ($\Gamma_0$) and subsequently monitored over 48 h to obtain the saturation load ($\Gamma_\infty$). Interfacial load exhibited a strong bulk concentration-dependent trend and was well described by a pseudo-first-order model. Both $\Gamma_0$ and $\Gamma_\infty$ followed sublinear scaling with concentration ($\Gamma_0$ ~ C^{0.21}$, $\Gamma_\infty$ ~ C^{0.12}$). Interfacial loads were largely independent of droplet diameter, with modest reductions in initial loading for the smallest droplets at low protein concentration. Measured loads exceeded idealized monolayer predictions and fell between bilayer and trilayer bounds, consistent with accumulation beyond a simplified monolayer model. Additionally, high-throughput mapping was performed across three proteins, seven concentrations, three pH values, and two ionic strengths, revealing that $\alpha$-Casein exhibited higher interfacial loads than $\beta$-Casein and Whey protein Isolate, with maximum adsorption near the isoelectric point and at elevated ionic strength. In summary, this study establishes a quantitative experimental framework for linking protein properties, formulation conditions, and interfacial behavior using monodisperse microfluidic emulsions, while requiring only milligram-scale protein quantities.
item.dc:creator: Varun Potdar (1Department of Chemical Engineering, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA), Alexander Favela (1Department of Chemical Engineering, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA), Michael Boehm (Motif FoodWorks, Inc., Boston, MA, USA), Stefan Baier (School of Chemical Engineering, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD 4072, Australia), Siva Vanapalli (1Department of Chemical Engineering, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA)

item.title: Swimming versus Screening: How Activity Reshapes the Ionic Cloud of a Charged Particle
item.description: arXiv:2610.38594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A major question in active matter is how interactions between particles are modified by activity. Here, we address this question for Coulomb interactions by considering a charged swimmer immersed in an electrolyte. A static charge is screened by an ionic cloud that decays over the Debye length $\lambda_D$. We show that the persistent motion of the swimmer can qualitatively modify the steady-state ionic charge-density profile. At low activity, the swimmer appears effectively quasistatic to the ions, and conventional Debye-H\"uckel screening is recovered. At higher activity, the ballistic-to-diffusive dynamics of the swimmer are reflected in distinct spatial regimes. A power-law decay is followed by a stretched-exponential decay at intermediate distances. At sufficiently large distances, exponential screening is restored, but with an increased screening length, $\lambda>\lambda_D$, revealing activity-induced underscreening. Thus, active motion modifies both the spatial form and the range of electrostatic screening. Our results motivate the study of active electrolytes composed of positively and negatively charged swimmers.
item.dc:creator: Tanmoy Chakraborty, Tomer Markovich, Ram M. Adar

item.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
item.description: arXiv:2610.39513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.
item.dc:creator: Ishan Amin, Yue Jian, Nitesh Kumar, Christine Zhang, Jianwei Lai, Casey S. Mezerkor, Aaron M. Melemed, Jonathan R. Thurston, Neil P. Dasgupta, J. David Bazak, Ethan J. Crumlin, Samuel Blau, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan

item.title: Multistable nematic liquid crystal pores as reconfigurable optical vortex metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.40123v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nematic liquid crystals confined in cylindrical pores adopt multiple stable director topologies --- radial, escaped, and arches --- each imprinting a distinct optical signature on transmitted circularly polarized light, with topological charge set by the projected director winding number, $\ell = 2m$. Using Landau--de Gennes and Jones-calculus modeling validated against micron-scale experiments, we show that this mechanism persists as the pore diameter shrinks toward the optical wavelength. However, full-wave Maxwell simulations of periodic sub-wavelength pore arrays reveal that the resulting vortex is a near-field phenomenon only: each topology imprints a distinguishable phase-singular signature --- differing in core multiplicity, core width, and ring amplitude --- directly below the pore array, but this signature does not survive propagation into the far field, where diffraction and inter-pore interference erase it within about one wavelength. Landau--de Gennes simulations further demonstrate that an applied electric field switches the pore between topologies, and hence between their near-field optical signatures. Because each topology is locally stable, sub-wavelength NLC pore arrays constitute an electrically reconfigurable, non-volatile platform for topology-encoded near-field optical readout, with potential application to optical labeling and anti-counterfeiting.
item.dc:creator: Claire Dor\'e, Brian Edwards, Nader Engheta, Kathleen J. Stebe

item.title: Odd Elasticity in Strain-Gradient Continua: Anisotropy Classification and Non-Hermitian Elastodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.40581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Odd elasticity extends continuum mechanics to active nonconservative systems containing internal energy sources, such as robotic active metamaterials with nonreciprocal feedback. Modeling these systems as effective continua requires relaxing Maxwell-Betti reciprocity, which results in stiffness tensors lacking major symmetry. In this contribution, we extend this framework to 3D strain-gradient odd elasticity to incorporate the length scales inherent in these heterogeneous systems. By applying the full hierarchy of 3D point-group symmetries along chiral and achiral branches, we derive the exhaustive set of fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-order odd elastic stiffness tensors. Further, utilizing the dynamic principle of virtual work, we formulate the equilibrium equations, higher-order boundary conditions, and the generalized acoustic tensor for elastodynamic analysis. The results demonstrate that nonreciprocal moduli survive even under full isotropy in the sixth-order stiffness, under hemitropy in the fifth-order stiffness, and under cubic symmetry in fourth-order stiffness. In contrast, the elastodynamic analysis reveals that under isotropic and hemitropic limits, despite the underlying odd stiffness moduli, the acoustic tensor remains unconditionally Hermitian. Non-Hermitian elastodynamics is shown to require anisotropy. By numerically analyzing a transversely hemitropic odd elastic continuum, we demonstrate that this symmetry reduction results in non-Hermitian elastodynamic phenomena including exceptional points in the dispersion spectra and active energy exchange through simultaneous amplification and attenuation of the elastic wave components. These results provide the necessary theoretical foundation for future multiscale homogenization frameworks for anisotropic strain-gradient active microstructures, and for the design of nonreciprocal strain-gradient metamaterials.
item.dc:creator: Payam Poorsolhjouy

item.title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization
item.description: arXiv:2610.40651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove stability of the asynchronous \textsf{R} squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chakraborty, Jong Yeon Lee

item.title: Active morphodynamics of intracellular organelles in the trafficking pathway
item.description: arXiv:2409.19084v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: From the Golgi apparatus to endosomes, organelles in the endomembrane system exhibit complex and varied morphologies that are often related to their function. These membrane-bound organelles operate far from equilibrium due to directed fluxes of trafficking vesicles, yet the physical principles governing the emergence and maintenance of these morphologies remain elusive. By coarse-graining the active mechanochemical cycles associated with individual fission and fusion events, we show how vesicular trafficking manifests at the hydrodynamic scale, generating not only fluxes of membrane area and encapsulated volume but also active stresses that mediate momentum transfer between an organelle and its cytosolic environment. The fluid and deformable nature of the bounding membrane gives rise to novel physics by coupling these nonequilibrium forces to organelle composition, morphology, and hydrodynamic flows. We demonstrate how both stable compartment drift and ramified sac-like morphologies, reminiscent of Golgi cisternal motion and shape, emerge from the same nonequilibrium dynamics of fission and fusion.
item.dc:creator: S. Alex Rautu, Richard G. Morris, Madan Rao

item.title: Rheologically tuned diffusion modulates quorum sensing in Vibrio fischeri
item.description: arXiv:2602.01786v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how the physical properties of a fluid influence bacterial behavior is essential for explaining how microorganisms interact with their environment and with animal hosts. Here, we examine how changes in fluid viscosity and rheological properties affect the locomotion of the marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri and its ability to produce luminescence through cell--cell communication. We track the three-dimensional motion of single cells in well-defined fluids with different physical properties and measure the luminescence emitted by cell populations. We find that fluids with higher viscosity cause V. fischeri to spend more time in a slower, turning-focused swimming mode, which reduces how effectively cells spread out and encounter the chemical signals required to activate luminescence. As a result, luminescence first increases and then decreases in Newtonian fluids, but decreases monotonically in fluids that exhibit non-Newtonian rheological behavior. Computer simulations based on our measurements confirm that the ability of cells to explore their surroundings plays a central role in determining when and how strongly they communicate. These findings reveal a direct link between the physical environment, bacterial movement, and collective behavior, and offer insight into how microorganisms adapt to complex fluid habitats, including those found inside animal hosts.
item.dc:creator: Chunhe Li, Zixiang Lin, Hongyi Bian, Anqi Li, Honyi Xin, Zijie Qu

item.title: Solvent-induced memory effects in a model electrolyte
item.description: arXiv:2605.06293v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The fluctuations of ions in polar solvents remain poorly understood theoretically due to the complex coupling between ionic motion and solvent polarization. Indeed, while all-atom resolution can be achieved in numerical simulations, analytical approaches require suitable levels of coarse-graining. In this work, we describe ions and solvent molecules as interacting Brownian particles and use stochastic density functional theory to derive a generalized Langevin equation for the ionic charge density, explicitly accounting for solvent-mediated memory effects. In the regime where there is a clear timescale separation between fast solvent and slow ion dynamics, we obtain simple expressions for dynamical charge structure factors, which are validated by BD simulations. For slow solvents, we predict an emerging two-step relaxation in ionic dynamics. These results provide a mesoscopic approach for ion-solvent dynamics and open pathways to study fluctuation-induced phenomena in electrolytes.
item.dc:creator: Sleeba Varghese, Benjamin Rotenberg, Pierre Illien

item.title: Inverse Design of Metainterfaces towards Static Friction Control: Beyond the Hertzian Limit
item.description: arXiv:2605.11012v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Programming the static friction of mechanical interfaces is critical for soft robotics, haptics, and precision gripping. Static friction is governed by the real contact area, and standard rough surfaces exhibit a linear area-load scaling inherent to classical models, severely restricting their functional range. Here, we propose a framework for the inverse design of tribological metainterfaces engineered for programmable contact behaviors. By utilizing general axisymmetric asperities, we unlock nonlinear macroscopic responses unattainable by standard Hertzian contacts. To solve the inverse problem, we embed a fully differentiable contact mechanics engine within a neural network and a quadratic optimizer. We leverage regularized physical gradients to automatically discover non-standard topographies that reproduce complex target contact laws, with only a few asperities in unit cells. The predicted designs are validated against high-fidelity Boundary Element Method (BEM) simulations. By front-loading computational costs during training, the neural surrogate yields near-instantaneous design inference, bypassing the bottlenecks of traditional multi-start optimization. This framework bridges data-driven optimization and rigorous physics, offering a scale-invariant pathway for the high-throughput discovery and real-time control of functional tribological surfaces.
item.dc:creator: Jacopo Bilotto, Arnav Singhal, Joaquin Garcia-Suarez, Ga\"etan Cortes, Lucas Fourel, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Molinari

item.title: Structure and energetics of grain boundaries in self-assembled double-gyroid block copolymer networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.26927v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) are ubiquitous defects in crystalline materials, but remain less explored in block copolymer ordered phases. Here, we develop a self-consistent field theory framework to investigate GB structure and energetics in double-gyroid (DG) diblock copolymer networks. Two energy landscapes are obtained for tilt and twist GBs as functions of GB orientations revealing multiple local minima. The lowest-energy GB among the sampled GBs is an asymmetric-tilt network-switching GB ($[\bar{1}\bar{1}1]$ ATNS) rather than the experimentally observed $(422)$ twin boundary (TB) among the sampled GBs. Comparative analyses of tilt ($[\bar{1}\bar{1}1]$, $[100]$ ATNS) and twist ($(422)$ TB, $[0\bar{1}\bar{1}]$ TNS) GBs reveal that, unlike enthalpy-dominated hard matter, GB stability in DG networks is entropy-driven. Twist-type GBs generate new nodes and disrupt nodal coplanarity, causing chain-packing frustration and entropy penalties. Although the [100] ATNS does not generate new nodes, its disruption of nodal coplanarity still incurs large entropy penalties. Conversely, the $[\bar{1}\bar{1}1]$ ATNS preserves favorable network connectivity and minimizes conformational constraints, making it the energetically preferred GB.
item.dc:creator: Jing Chen, Aiping Zhu, Dan Wei, An-Chang Shi, Kai Jiang

item.title: Hybrid Dynamical Simulation Reveals Apparent Stiffening of Flexible Protein Lattices Driving Membrane Bending
item.description: arXiv:2607.06378v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Membrane-deforming protein lattices play a central role in essential and pathogenic remodeling processes, including clathrin-mediated endocytosis and viral budding. Simulating these systems at biologically relevant length and time scales requires mesoscale approaches that preserve structural detail. We present a hybrid simulation framework that couples a particle-based flexible protein lattice to a continuum membrane model, enabling systematic investigation of how lattice geometry and rigidity influence membrane remodeling. We validate the coupled model by comparing simulation results with theoretical predictions for membranes under increasing tension. Using buckling-based deformations of pre-assembled clathrin lattices, we quantify the lattice flexural rigidity and establish a direct relationship between the force constants in the coarse-grained energy function and the emergent lattice mechanics. We then compare this flexural rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$, to an effective rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$, commonly used in continuum descriptions of sphere-forming protein assemblies. Although $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$ is set solely by the energy function, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on lattice size and connectivity, with the two measures converging for weakly-connected lattices. As a result, with lattice growth, the effective rigidity relevant for spherical bud formation increases and the relaxation timescale decreases. This size-dependent stiffening highlights the importance of structural details in interpreting lattice mechanics and cautions against assuming a single constant stiffness. We demonstrate the generality of the method by applying it to pre-assembled viral lattices generated with reaction-diffusion simulations. This work provides a validated framework for simulating deformable protein assemblies of diverse geometry coupled to membrane dynamics and remodeling.
item.dc:creator: Samuel L. Foley, Margaret E. Johnson

item.title: Fast temperature up steps as a test of the Tool-Narayanaswamy formalism
item.description: arXiv:2607.15988v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigated the aging dynamics of a glass-forming liquid triethyl-2-acetylcitrate (TEAC), following fast temperature up steps with amplitudes ranging from 0.3 to 13.6 K. The initial states were either at equilibrium or prepared at increasing levels of out-of-equilibrium through a prior down step experiment. Our goal was to test the predictive power of the Tool-Narayanaswamy (TN) formalism which assumes that the non-linear re-equilibration of a liquid can be linked to its linear response to a small perturbation. We determined the TN parameters for steps with small to moderate amplitude ($\leq 3.3$~K) and crucially took advantage of down step aging experiments below the glass transition temperature to constrain the determination of the equilibrium relaxation time. We tested the TN predictions and found very good agreement for differences in fictive temperature characterizing the distance from equilibrium as high as 10~K. For larger steps, however, the prediction progressively fails to capture the aging dynamics. This likely indicates that the re-equilibration mechanism is no longer related to the equilibrium dynamics. Finally, we discuss the possibility of obtaining a general criterion for the limit of validity of the TN formalism, which we compare to other systems from the literature.
item.dc:creator: Armand Rykner, Fran\c{c}ois Ladieu, Marceau H\'enot

item.title: Structure, Diffusion, and Relaxation in a Charge-Neutral ProTalpha-Histone H1 Condensate
item.description: arXiv:2607.29639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Condensates formed by oppositely charged intrinsically disordered proteins provide model systems for understanding how transient electrostatic interactions govern structure and dynamics in biomolecular assemblies. Here we investigate a nearly charge-neutral condensate composed of 50 Prothymosin alpha (ProTalpha) and 40 Histone H1 molecules using a single-bead-per-residue coarse-grained model combining the HPS hydropathy model for disordered regions with a Go model for the globular domain of Histone H1 under NPT conditions at pressures from 2 to 12 bar. We find that chain dimensions, including the radius of gyration (Rg), end-to-end distance (Ree), and their ratio R, are insensitive to pressure, indicating that chain conformations remain largely unchanged over the pressure range studied. Histone H1 exhibits systematically larger values of R than ProTalpha because of its globular-core plus disordered-tail architecture. Translational diffusion coefficients decrease monotonically with pressure, from approximately 0.22 to 0.06 nm^2/ns, with substantial chain-to-chain heterogeneity comparable to the mean diffusion coefficient. Chain relaxation follows a stretched exponential with beta less than 1 that decreases with pressure. ProTalpha relaxation times of approximately 12 to 40 ns obey Rouse scaling, whereas Histone H1 deviates because of the internal constraint imposed by its globular domain. ProTalpha-Histone H1 contact lifetimes of approximately 0.43 to 0.56 ns are much shorter than the Rouse relaxation time, placing the system firmly in the fast-exchange regime where transient electrostatic contacts renormalize chain friction rather than acting as permanent cross-links, consistent with the moderate stretching exponent beta of approximately 0.55 to 0.70 observed across all pressures.
item.dc:creator: Aniket Bhattacharya

item.title: Liquid crystalline order and its impact on shape evolution of fluid lipid membranes
item.description: arXiv:2609.40113v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider extensions of the classical curvature-elasticity free energy for a fluid lipid membrane, explicitly treating the liquid crystal structure of the membrane, which results from the lipid molecules that are, on average, oriented normal to the surface. Locally varying liquid crystal order leads to local variations in bending rigidities and surface viscosity and thus influences the shape evolution. This provides a multiscale coupling between the local membrane mechanics on the level of the lipids and the mesoscopic length and time scales of biological functions. Numerical simulations in the one-constant approximation demonstrate the impact of local membrane mechanics on the emerging equilibrium shapes. These shapes not only depend on the specified conserved surface area and enclosed volume, as for the classical curvature-elasticity free energy, but also the elastic parameter and are characterized by a reduced liquid crystal order at highly curved regions. The modified shapes and their varying liquid crystal order, as function of curvature, provide experimentally testable properties. Exploring the dynamic evolution demonstrate a tight coupling of tangential flow, shape evolution and liquid crystalline order. We further point to model extensions towards lipid phase separation and asymmetric lipid bilayers and biological implications.
item.dc:creator: Ingo Nitschke, Maik Porrmann, Axel Voigt

item.title: From Action Principle to Stochastic Thermodynamics of Elastic and Viscous Active Matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.21835v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motivated by the complex material properties of living matter, we derive a framework of stochastic thermo- and elastodynamics for active materials from the classical principle of least action and the Rayleighian formalism for external forces. Our approach couples the local barycentric collective coordinate and the streaming velocity as the canonical conjugate pair, which unifies various descriptions of elastic and viscous soft matter, including Helfrich theory for lipid membranes, linear and nonlinear elasticity of thin shells and deformable droplets, as well as hydrodynamics of active and passive fluids. The Lagrangian mechanics of collective field variables permits direct applications of the results and theorems from statistical mechanics to existing models of complex soft and living matter. To illustrate the potential applications of stochastic elastodynamics in biology, we derive and simulate a boundary-driven deformation model of an elastic cell nucleus in the presence of fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Valentina Barletta, Michele Lupini, Ian D. Estabrook, Laeschkir W\"urthner, Isabella R. Graf, Caren Norden, Lamberto Rondoni, Anna Erzberger, Roman Belousov

item.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Microgel Glasses via Particle Stiffness
item.description: arXiv:2610.29389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, particle stiffness governs deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, and thereby dictates the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses, and establish Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.
item.dc:creator: Sonali Vasant Kawale, Ranjini Bandyopadhyay

item.title: Dynamic Peach-Koehler self-force, inertia, and radiation damping of a regularized dislocation
item.description: arXiv:2005.12704v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The elastodynamic Peach-Koehler force is computed for a fully-regularized straight dislocation with isotropic core in continuum isotropic elastic elasticity, in compact forms involving partial mass or impulsion functions relative to shear and compressional waves. The force accounts for both dynamic radiation damping and inertia. The expressions are valid indifferently for subsonic or supersonic velocities. Results are compared with the case of a flat-core dislocation of the Peierls-Eshelby type, for a motion of jump from rest to constant velocity. In the steady-state limit, the Lagrangian function relevant to expressing the force in the flat-core case must be replaced by a related but different function for the regularized dislocation. However, by suitably defining the regularizing dislocation width, the steady-state limits of the force for the fully-regularized and flat-core dislocations can be matched exactly.
item.dc:creator: Yves-Patrick Pellegrini

item.title: Activation and Avalanche Length Scales in the Finite-Temperature Creep of an Elastic Interface
item.description: arXiv:2604.17600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the creep dynamics of a driven elastic line at finite temperature, well below the depinning threshold. We show that creep is governed by two distinct length scales. The first, $\ell_{\mathrm{opt}}$, corresponds to the optimal activated rearrangements that control the dynamics' bottleneck and remains essentially temperature-independent. The second, $\ell_{\mathrm{av}}$, characterizes the spatial extent of thermally activated avalanches and grows as temperature decreases. By combining structural and dynamical observables, we show that $\ell_{\mathrm{av}}$ governs both the crossover in the structure factor and the growth of the four-point dynamical susceptibility, while the relaxation time remains controlled by activation over large barriers associated with $\ell_{\mathrm{opt}}$. We find that the avalanche scale follows $\ell_{\mathrm{av}}(T)\sim T^{-\nu_{\mathrm{dep}}}$, thereby selecting a unique scenario among competing theoretical predictions. These results establish a unified picture of finite-temperature creep in which activation controls temporal scales while depinning criticality governs spatial correlations.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Russo, Ezequiel E. Ferrero, Alejandro B. Kolton, Alberto Rosso, Damien Vandembroucq

item.title: Link length and energy fluctuations in extensible freely jointed chains
item.description: arXiv:2605.12333v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The freely jointed chain is often applied to model the thermodynamics of single polymer chains, but the traditional formulation of the model lacks internal energy changes due to bond stretching. For this reason, the extensible freely jointed chain model includes a potential energy function, typically harmonic, that governs the length of each link in the chain. Among the other quantities of interest that are subject to thermal fluctuations, these link lengths and energies too fluctuate about their ensemble average values. Since a plethora of models for polymer chains and networks incorporate chain dissociation as a function of either link length or energy, these fluctuations are crucial to understand and quantify. Motivated by this fact, fluctuations in link length and energy are analyzed within a freely jointed chain under an applied force. These fluctuations are quantified through their average values, standard deviations, and probability distributions. Across all values, asymptotically correct analytic relations and their less ergonomic exact counterparts are introduced. The asymptotic relations are verified to be accurate through direct comparison and to be correct within transcendentally small terms through error analysis. In certain cases, the fluctuations are shown to be approximately normally distributed. Hereafter, model components predicated on link length or energy ought to account for these fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Buche

item.title: Modified Family-Vicsek Scaling and Probability Distributions for Brownian Castle Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2607.13922v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Brownian Castle is a new interface growth model that is a variation on the well-known ballistic deposition model that results in an entirely new universality class. We present numerical verification that the interface width for BC interfaces displays modified Family-Vicsek scaling properties up to finite size corrections. Specifically, we find a growth exponent of $\beta=0.470 \pm 0.012$ and a roughness exponent of $\alpha=1.01 \pm 0.018$. The scaling is modified at short times with a size scaling exponent that described the early time dependence of interface width on length. The probability distribution of heights for the BC interface shows significant deviations from simple Gaussian behavior and the probability distribution of height changes shows a Cauchy-Lorentz form consistent with expectations for a process involving relatively large jumps.
item.dc:creator: Noah Sublett, Charles Sutton, Benjamin Long, Daniel B. Dougherty

item.title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.31924v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models and spatial resolution. Here we demonstrate a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model that establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit. We discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from a pinned state directly at the channel-dielectric interface of an organic transistor, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics that contradict models based on substrate patterning. This non-destructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final configuration opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.
item.dc:creator: Harlan Heilman, Em Biegler, Sushil Adhikari, Victor Murcia, Tanner Melody, Fred Woodall, Lars Thomsen, Obaid Alqahtani, Brian A. Collins

item.title: Stability reversal, activated escape, and mechanical response of negative-mobility particles
item.description: arXiv:2610.36884v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding the fluctuations and response of particles in potential landscapes is a fundamental problem in nonequilibrium statistical physics. Here, we investigate how negative mobility reshapes the stochastic behavior of a particle moving in a mechanical potential landscape. We consider a one-dimensional overdamped particle subject to additive noise, with mobility that is negative at weak forces and positive at strong forces. In a potential well, negative mobility destabilizes the mechanical potential minimum and produces bimodal localization at two off-center positions. The same stability reversal transforms conventional Kramers escape from a potential well into a two-stage escape process involving an intermediate metastable state. When an additional spatially uniform force is applied, the mechanical perturbation translates rather than tilts the effective double well, yielding a positive response dominated at weak noise by intrawell relaxation, even though slow interwell switching dominates spontaneous positional fluctuations. These findings reveal how negative mobility reshapes the interplay among mechanical landscapes, stochastic stability, and response.
item.dc:creator: Junteng Li, Zhihong You
